title: ACGME Duty Hour Violations | Build the Rules In
description: Most ACGME duty hour violations trace back to the build. Scheduling Wizard builds the duty hour rules into the schedule itself, so there is less to find afterwards.
h1: Fewer Duty Hour Problems, Because the Rules Go In First
paragraph: Most duty hour problems start in the build. We put the rules in while the schedule is created, so there is less to find afterwards.

cta.title: Stop Checking the Schedule After You Build It
cta.description: Book a call to talk through your scheduling needs and learn how Scheduling Wizard works. Join 30+ departments across 20+ hospitals and practices that have us build their call, block, clinic and shift schedules.

faq.answer: The most common ACGME duty hour violations are exceeding the 80-hour weekly limit once moonlighting is counted, not providing eight hours off between duty periods, breaking the 14-hour rest window after 24-hour call, miscounting the one-day-off-in-seven average, and exceeding the 24-hour cap on continuous duty. Most of them trace back to how the schedule was built rather than to anyone's intent.
faq.question: What are the most common ACGME duty hour violations in residency programs?

faq.answer: We apply the duty hour rules while the schedule is built rather than producing one and checking it afterwards. The 80-hour average, the rest requirements, the 24-hour cap and your subspecialty's own rules are all part of the build. We work from the requirements your program tells us apply, and if something needs to change we redraft.
faq.question: How does Scheduling Wizard prevent ACGME duty hour violations?

faq.answer: If a duty hour violation is identified after a schedule is published, the affected portion of the schedule must be revised and redistributed, which can disrupt the entire program. Scheduling Wizard addresses this upstream by building compliance into the schedule at creation time. For mid-year changes that introduce new rules, our team can re-optimize affected portions of the schedule without requiring a full rebuild.
faq.question: What happens if a duty hour violation is found after a schedule is published?

faq.answer: Yes. Subspecialty-specific ACGME duty hour rules are built into the schedule itself. ACGME compliance is the most common question asked during onboarding, and the service is designed to handle the nuances that vary across residency and fellowship programs. Programs should communicate their specific requirements during the rule submission process so our team can apply the correct rules for their specialty.
faq.question: Does Scheduling Wizard know the ACGME rules for my specific subspecialty?

faq.answer: Schedules are delivered as ready-to-use Excel or Google Sheets files. If you want one, we can also build a custom live viewing link for your program, designed around your schedules. Many Scheduling Wizard clients upload these finished files directly into your existing platform for day-to-day viewing and access. Scheduling Wizard handles the schedule creation and optimization, while you publish it where you already do. There is no new software for your program to learn or operate.
faq.question: How are schedules delivered and can we use them with your existing platform?

faq.answer: This is where a lot of problems start. When a chief resident rotates out, what they knew about the rules, the requests and past decisions usually leaves with them. Scheduling Wizard keeps all of it, so the incoming chief inherits a working schedule and the reasoning behind it rather than a blank spreadsheet.
faq.question: Who is responsible for scheduling when chief residents rotate annually?
